The human amygdala and the induction and experience of fear
Feinstein, Adolphs, Damasio & Tranel (2011) · Current Biology 21(1), 34–38
Blue notes = updates from Feinstein et al. (2013), Nature Neuroscience
Presenter: Yaqi Hu · 10.13.2026
The question
Is the amygdala needed to trigger fear, and to feel it?
STIMULUS
External threat
Snakes, a haunted house, scary films
FEAR INDUCTION
Fear state triggered
Measured by behavior: avoidance, withdrawal
FEAR EXPERIENCE
Fear is felt
Measured by self-report
Prediction · no amygdala → the fear state is never induced → the feeling never follows
Feinstein et al. (2011), p. 1–2

Patient SM
SM
44-year-old woman
Urbach–Wiethe disease: rare genetic disorder
Studied 20+ years; profile stable
Intact
IQ, memory, language, perception
Knows what fear is
Sees fear in voices, bodies, films

Impaired
Fear conditioning
Fear in static faces
Social judgment, personal space
Insight into her own deficit
Key · fearless, but not emotionless, and she understands fear
Feinstein et al. (2011) p. 1–2; Supplement S1–S2
The lesion
Focal, bilateral, nearly complete
Yellow boxes = calcified amygdalae, both sides · Blue circles = newer putamen lesions
A = at study onset; B = 10 years earlier
DAMAGED
Both amygdalae (calcium deposits), plus a small area of entorhinal cortex and white matter
INTACT
Hippocampus · insula · vmPFC · hypothalamus · brainstem (PAG)
STABLE
Unchanged for 20+ years; onset likely late childhood
2013 · twins AM and BG with the same disease and lesions join SM as test cases
Supplement, Figure S1 and caption (p. S8)

Results · Life history
No fear since Urbach-Wiethe calcifications 
Before 10
Felt fear: the dark, a cornering Doberman
About 10
Calcification typically begins
Age 30
Knife at her throat: calm, walked home
Age 44
No adult fear found anywhere
Key · robbed at knife- and gunpoint, nearly killed (police-verified): no urgency, no avoidance, only anger
2013 · CO₂ made her feel fear and panic, the first time since childhood; the authors' "immune to PTSD" idea gets more complicated
Feinstein et al. (2011) p. 4; Supplement S3–S5; Feinstein et al. (2013) p. 2–3
Proposed mechanism
A broken link between perceiving and fearing
INTACT
Sensory cortex
Sees the snake
LESIONED
Amygdala
Triggers the fear state
INTACT
Hypothalamus, PAG
Run the fear program
INTACT
Body → insula
Felt as fear
WHY OTHER EMOTIONS SURVIVE
Prefrontal and cingulate cortex reach hypothalamus and brainstem directly, bypassing the amygdala
2013 · A SECOND ROUTE
Internal CO₂ reaches brainstem and insula directly: fear and panic without the amygdala
Key · no fear state is triggered, so there is nothing to feel
Feinstein et al. (2011) p. 4–5; Supplement p. S5–S6; Feinstein et al. (2013) p. 3–4
Conclusion
Without the amygdala, outside threats cannot trigger fear, and with no fear state there is no feeling
Necessary trigger
For fear of threats in the environment
Specific to fear
Sadness, anger, disgust, happiness remain
Arousal is not fear
Excitement and curiosity remain; approach replaces avoidance
Limits · one patient · lesion not purely amygdala · childhood onset · no controls or physiology in field settings · past events rely on recall
Feinstein et al. (2011) Conclusions p. 4–5; Supplement "Limitations" p. S7

Discussion
Questions from the board
1
Arousal or fear? Was SM’s excitement relabeled arousal, or was fear never triggered?
No physiology in 2011 · 2013: anticipatory arousal missing, reactive arousal intact
2
Brain vs feeling: if amygdala activity drops, does felt fear drop with it?
SM lost both · CO₂ fear needed no amygdala · neurofeedback can lower one without the other
3
Lesion or personality? Is her “compulsive curiosity” the damage, or who she is?
Klüver–Bucy parallel, as in Radiolab’s Kevin · no field controls · pre-lesion personality unknown
4
Knowing vs fearing: is fear about danger itself, or predicting what comes next?
SM knows snakes bite, still reaches · Kevin knew it was wrong, couldn’t stop · 2013: no anticipation
5
Where and when: would another subregion, or adult onset, give a different profile?
SM: fearless approach · Kevin: compulsions after adult surgery · childhood vs adult onset

Looking ahead
SM shows what happens when the fear trigger is failed. Could we weaken one fear by changing the memory it runs on?
